en: Itivuttaka 90: Tikanipāta, Pañcamavagga Thus it was said by the Blessed One, so I have heard: “Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The person who is like a stone pillar, the person who is like a water jar, and the person who is like a lotus. And how, monks, is one a person like a stone pillar? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of hatred toward his mother, his father, his brother, his sister, and his friends and companions; he dwells with a mind full of hatred toward recluses and brahmins, and toward other beings as well. This, monks, is called a person like a stone pillar. And how, monks, is one a person like a water jar? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind free from hatred toward his mother, his father, his brother, his sister, and his friends and companions; he dwells with a mind free from hatred toward recluses and brahmins, and toward other beings as well. Yet he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This, monks, is called a person like a water jar. And how, monks, is one a person like a lotus? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind free from hatred toward his mother, his father, his brother, his sister, and his friends and companions; he dwells with a mind free from hatred toward recluses and brahmins, and toward other beings as well. And he understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This, monks, is called a person like a lotus. These, monks, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus it was said by the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, soon after the Blessed One had departed, the venerable Ānanda addressed the monks: “Friends, the Blessed One has spoken in brief regarding these three persons, and he has explained their detailed meaning. Listen, friends, and pay close attention; I shall speak. “Yes, friend,” those monks replied to the venerable Ānanda. The venerable Ānanda said this: “And how, friends, is one a person like a stone pillar? [As before]... This, friends, is called a person like a stone pillar. And how, friends, is one a person like a water jar? [As before]... This, friends, is called a person like a water jar. And how, friends, is one a person like a lotus? [As before]... This, friends, is called a person like a lotus. Thus, friends, the Blessed One spoke in brief regarding these three persons, and he has explained their detailed meaning. “Excellent, friend! Excellent, friend! said those monks to the venerable Ānanda. They rejoiced and were delighted in what the venerable Ānanda had said. Then they paid homage to the venerable Ānanda and, keeping him on their right, they departed. Then, not long after those monks had left, the venerable Sāriputta approached the venerable Ānanda, exchanged greetings with him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the venerable Sāriputta said to the venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, when the Blessed One spoke in brief regarding these three persons and explained their detailed meaning, what did the Blessed One mean? “Friend Sāriputta, the Blessed One spoke of these three persons based on the underlying tendency toward lust, the underlying tendency toward aversion, and the underlying tendency toward delusion. And how, friend, is one a person like a stone pillar? Here, friend, a certain person dwells with a mind full of lust for his mother, his father, his brother, his sister, and his friends and companions; he dwells with a mind full of lust for recluses and brahmins, and toward other beings as well. He dwells with a mind full of aversion toward his mother, his father, his brother, his sister, and his friends and companions; he dwells with a mind full of aversion toward recluses and brahmins, and toward other beings as well. He dwells with a mind full of delusion regarding his mother, his father, his brother, his sister, and his friends and companions; he dwells with a mind full of delusion toward recluses and brahmins, and toward other beings as well. This, friend, is called a person like a stone pillar. And how, friend, is one a person like a water jar? Here, friend, a certain person dwells with a mind free from lust for his mother, his father, his brother, his sister, and his friends and companions; he dwells with a mind free from lust for recluses and brahmins, and toward other beings as well. He dwells with a mind free from aversion toward his mother, his father, his brother, his sister, and his friends and companions; he dwells with a mind free from aversion toward recluses and brahmins, and toward other beings as well. He dwells with a mind free from delusion regarding his mother, his father, his brother, his sister, and his friends and companions; he dwells with a mind free from delusion toward recluses and brahmins, and toward other beings as well. Yet he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This, friend, is called a person like a water jar. And how, friend, is one a person like a lotus? Here, friend, a certain person dwells with a mind free from lust for his mother, his father, his brother, his sister, and his friends and companions; he dwells with a mind free from lust for recluses and brahmins, and toward other beings as well. He dwells with a mind free from aversion toward his mother, his father, his brother, his sister, and his friends and companions; he dwells with a mind free from aversion toward recluses and brahmins, and toward other beings as well. He dwells with a mind free from delusion regarding his mother, his father, his brother, his sister, and his friends and companions; he dwells with a mind free from delusion toward recluses and brahmins, and toward other beings as well. And he understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This, friend, is called a person like a lotus. Thus, friend, the Blessed One spoke of these three persons based on the underlying tendency toward lust, the underlying tendency toward aversion, and the underlying tendency toward delusion. “It is wonderful, friend Ānanda! It is marvelous, friend Ānanda! How well this has been stated by the venerable Ānanda. For the Blessed One spoke of these three persons based on the underlying tendency toward lust, the underlying tendency toward aversion, and the underlying tendency toward delusion. And the venerable Ānanda has now explained it in detail. Thus it was said by the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. And that is how it was said by the Blessed One, so I have heard.
The Discourse on Supreme Confidence.
This was said by the Blessed One; "So I have heard" was said by the Arahant.
"Monks, there are these three supreme confidences."
Which three?
Monks, whatever beings there may be—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed; whether with form or formless;
whether percipient, non-percipient, or neither percipient nor non-percipient—the Tathāgata is declared to be the foremost among them.
He is an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Those, monks, who have faith in the Buddha have faith in the foremost.
And for those who have faith in the foremost, the result is foremost.
"Monks, whatever phenomena there are, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion (*virāga*) is declared to be their foremost;

that is to say, the crushing of intoxication, the removal of thirst, the uprooting of attachment, the cutting off of the cycle of existence, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, and Nibbāna.
Those, monks, who have faith in the phenomena of dispassion have faith in the foremost."
Furthermore, for those with faith, the foremost [deed] has the foremost result as its maturation.
Monks, of all assemblies or groups whatsoever, the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples is declared to be the foremost;
that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this is the Blessed One’s Saṅgha of disciples, worthy of offerings.
He is worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
Those, monks, who have faith in the Saṅgha have faith in the foremost.
And for those who have faith in the foremost, the result is foremost.
“Monks, these are the three foremost confidences.
Thus the Blessed One spoke. With reference to this, it is said:
“Truly, for those who have faith in the foremost,
who understand the foremost Dhamma,
and who have faith in the foremost Buddha— ”
To those supreme ones worthy of offerings,
who have faith in the highest Dharma—
the bliss of dispassion and tranquility—
For those who have faith in the foremost Saṅgha,
the unsurpassed field of merit,
giving gifts to the most excellent, [there is great fruit].
Supreme merit increases;
supreme are longevity, beauty, fame,
renown, happiness, and strength.
The wise giver of the best,
established in the highest Dhamma,
whether become a deva or a human, [attains the highest state].
"One who has reached the summit rejoices.
This meaning was also spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
First.
